sections.overview: Paragonimus westermani is a parasitic flatworm commonly called the Oriental Lung Fluke. It is one of the most frequently reported Paragonimus species in human infections.
sections.identification: Adults are robust, oval flukes about 7.5–12 mm long and 4–6 mm wide. Their eggs have a thick shell and a visible lid-like operculum.
sections.habitat: The species is reported from Southeast Asia and Japan. Mature worms usually become encapsulated in the lungs of mammalian hosts, including humans and other mammals.
sections.diet: Its exact food intake is not detailed in the sources consulted.
sections.behavior: Its larvae pass through a freshwater snail and then a crustacean such as a crab or crayfish. Mammals become infected when they eat the crustacean raw or insufficiently cooked.
sections.reproduction: Eggs leave the mammalian host in sputum or, after being swallowed, in faeces. In water they develop before larvae enter the snail host. CDC describes adult flukes as hermaphroditic.
sections.ecology: More than 30 species of Paragonimus are known; P. westermani is a common cause of human infection in Asia.
sections.conservation: No conservation assessment was located in the references consulted.
